title: Under review.
summary: The introduction establishes that shaping (curriculum learning) is critical for effective learning in animals and humans, but lacks a quantitative theory. The paper aims to develop a theory of compositional task learning in RL using teacher-student frameworks and statistical mechanics tools.

title: Main contributions
summary: This section lists the paper's main contributions: deriving asymptotically exact ODEs for compositional RL in a teacher-student setup, analyzing primitives pre-training versus vanilla training curricula, and showing that curriculum learning yields faster learning and robustness to noise.

title: Related Work
summary: The related work section surveys the teacher-student framework and statistical physics approaches to learning dynamics, curriculum learning in neuroscience and machine learning, and prior work on compositionality in RL and other domains like vision and language.

title: Compositional Learning and Primitives
summary: This section defines the compositional learning model using K primitive RL perceptrons combined via a context vector in a teacher-student framework. It derives sparse-reward learning rules (analogous to REINFORCE) for both individual primitives and the compositional task.

title: Learning Dynamics in Different Curricula
summary: The section introduces two curricula—primitives pre-training and vanilla training—and derives a set of ODEs in the high-dimensional limit (N→∞) that describe the evolution of order parameters (alignment, norm) governing generalisation error.

title: Primitives Pre-training
summary: This section analyzes primitives pre-training, showing that the primitive learning timescale τ_primitive is exponential in episode length T due to sparse rewards. After primitives reach expert level, compositional generalization proceeds relatively quickly.

title: Compositional generalization.
summary: This section derives the timescale for compositional generalization after primitives pre-training, showing total training time is dominated by primitive training for large T. The initial alignment between student context V₀ and target context V* plays a key role in generalization speed.

title: Vanilla Training
summary: The vanilla training section describes a student learning the compositional task directly, noting that each primitive is learned on a different timescale while context learning occurs at a similar rate across primitives.

title: Initial context alignment drives primitive learning speed.
summary: This section shows how initial context alignment (V₀ₖV*ₖ) modulates primitive learning timescales in vanilla training, with better alignment leading to faster learning. It derives an approximate closed-form solution for early Rₖ dynamics and the characteristic timescale.

title: Initial context alignment drives primitive learning speed.
summary: The final section discusses the emergence of multiplicative primitive learning, where the assumption R_{k'≠k}≈0 breaks down as overall alignment grows, causing an interaction effect between primitives during vanilla learning.

title: C.2. Compositional Generalisation after pre-training
summary: This section derives constrained update rules for V_k using a Lagrange multiplier, obtaining explicit expressions for the gradient updates of V_k and R_k that satisfy the imposed constraint.

title: Figure 1 .
summary: Figure 1 illustrates the teacher-student setup for compositional tasks with K primitives, where each primitive is modeled by a fixed teacher network and a learnable student network, with outputs blended using fixed teacher context.

title: Figure 2 .
summary: Figure 2 shows learning dynamics for primitives pre-training curriculum, including single-primitive dynamics approximated by ODEs, compositional generalization dynamics across different T and initial cosine similarities, and total training time comparisons between pre-training and generalization phases.

title: Figure 3 .
summary: Figure 3 analyzes vanilla learning dynamics, showing that ODE approximations match numerical simulations, initial context overlap controls primitive learning delay, and a multiplicative learning effect causes later primitives to learn faster when earlier ones are better trained.

title: Figure 4 .
summary: Figure 4 demonstrates that primitives pre-training curriculum learning achieves faster learning compared to vanilla learning, with the training time ratio varying by initial cosine similarity of context weights.

title: Figure 5 .
summary: Figure 5 examines robustness to noise in curriculum learning, showing that primitives pre-training is more robust than vanilla training, particularly when noise in the context update is large.
